newsitem.title: PERU: Peru frees 114 people wrongly jailed for terrorism.
newsitem.headline: Peru frees 114 people wrongly jailed for terrorism.

text.p: Peru on Wednesday released 114 prisoners jailed unjustly for terrorism by "faceless" courts during the state's ongoing war against leftist guerrillas.

The announcement marked the restart of a judicial review of the situation of hundreds of jailed Peruvians that the government suspended during the hostage crisis when Marxist rebels seized the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima.

For four months, Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) guerrillas demanded the release of some 400 jailed comrades in exchange for 72 VIP hostages, but troops stormed the embassy residence in April and killed all 14 rebels.
Wednesday's decree, signed by President Alberto Fujimori, came as a surprise for euphoric prisoners and their families.
"I only found out this morning. I nearly fainted when they told me. After so much injustice, it's hard to believe," said Maria Elena Rodriguez Shauz as she walked out of Lima's Chorrillos prison.

Rodriguez said she was treated "badly, very badly" in prison where she spent 11 months, but added: "I give thanks to God, to Christ, because I am innocent and everyone who turned their backs on me will know it now."
Her son, Rafael Guerra Rodriquez, hugged and kissed his mother as she emerged from the prison's black steel door with 13 other tired but happy-looking women carrying their belongings in plastic bags.

"I have three brothers and sisters waiting for my mother, and when they see her walk in, we'll all jump for joy," he said. "This is the happiest day of my life, I never thought I would see my mother free."
As armed guards looked on, the women, some crying, pushed through a crowd of reporters to reach their loved-ones.

Belgian Catholic priest Hubert Lanssiers, a commission member, hailed the action as "tremendous, extraordinary" after such a long gap since the last releases in October. The government had released about 100 prisoners up to October on recommendations by the commission.
"There was another list ready before (MRTA leader Nestor) Cerpa went in, which set everything back," he said, referring to the MRTA's Dec. 17 assault on the Japanese embassy.

Justice Minister Carlos Hermoza Moya said Fujimori, with the hostage crisis behind him, had restarted the review process because of "his willingness to resolve the situation of these people who were condemned on the basis of evidence taken to an exaggerated degree by the tribunals."

Hermoza said another 200 prisoners would likely be freed in coming months, although human rights group say up to 800 more innocent people are still in jail on terrorism charges. Most of the falsely accused prisoners were put behind bars by controversial "faceless" courts, whose anonymous judges wear hoods or sit behind one-way screens to protect their identity.
Despite errors committed by those courts and criticism from rights groups at home and abroad, Congress agreed late last year to extend the tribunals at least until mid-October.
The government argues that the courts are still necessary in the war against the MRTA and the larger Maoist guerrilla movement, Shining Path.
